item.title: On Small Universal Reversible Turing Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.00153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A reversible Turing machine (RTM) is a Turing machine in which every instantaneous description has at most one predecessor. Writing URTM(m,n) for a universal RTM with m states and n symbols, we construct URTM(3,600), URTM(4,41), URTM(5,37), URTM(6,30), URTM(7,28), URTM(8,21), and URTM(85,2); each of them has fewer states or fewer symbols than each of the nine URTMs in Morita's book (2017). They come from improved versions of Morita's conversions to three states, to four states, and to two symbols; for example, the improved conversion to three states uses O(mn^2) symbols instead of O(m^2n^3). We also show that the halting problem of RTMs with at most two states is decidable for finite instantaneous descriptions, so that no RTM with at most two states is universal under any notion of universality that reduces the halting problem of Turing machines to it by a computable encoding into finite instantaneous descriptions; in particular, there is no URTM with at most two states in our formalization of Morita's definition. We also show that no three-state, two-symbol RTM is universal in that formalization.
item.dc:creator: T. Yokoyama

item.title: Classification of non-Leibnizian Strings
item.description: arXiv:2611.01625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leibnizian ideas in foundations of physics has enjoyed a renewed interest. Cyclic string ontology in Wolfram Model multiway rewriting systems has been found to encode finite dimensional quantum systems where what are called as Leibnizian strings have been employed. It has then become important to classify strings in terms of their ability to correspond to a monadic interpretation \`a la Leibniz. The definition of Leibnizian strings are rather quite non-linear and for that purpose we classify non-Leibnizian strings for which there is a simpler criterion on maximal neighborhoods of characters. If a string is not non-Leibnizian then it must be Leibnizian. We found out three canonical forms of non-Leibnizian strings and noted that two of them are context-free languages whereas one is not.
item.dc:creator: Furkan Semih D\"undar

item.title: The Scope Grammar of Natural-Language Rules: Counting and Enumerating Readings modulo Logical Equivalence
item.description: arXiv:2611.01825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A rule written for people fixes its atomic conditions and connectives but leaves open how the connectives are bracketed, and each bracketing is a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose. We study the scope grammar, a deliberately ambiguous context-free grammar whose derivation trees are the readings of a connective skeleton and whose quotient by logical equivalence is what matters downstream. A skeleton with $k$ binary connectives has $C_k$ derivation trees, the $k$-th Catalan number, but far fewer logically distinct readings. For the positive, repetition-free fragment we make the gap exact: through the uniqueness of the read-once normal form we characterize the realizable normal forms by lowest common ancestors and count them with a two-label recurrence over the operator word, verified against exhaustive enumeration up to eleven atoms. The count is invariant under reversal and $\wedge/\vee$ duality; a skeleton is ambiguous if and only if it uses both $\wedge$ and $\vee$, a one-pass test; and the number of classes is at least $2^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}$. Up to fifteen atoms the alternating pattern is the worst case; its count has a cubic generating function, is the 3-Schr\"oder sequence (OEIS A137842), and grows with base $\varphi^{5/2}\approx3.330$, below the Catalan base 4. We reduce maximality to an inequality on increments, verified to sixteen atoms, and explain why local exchange arguments cannot prove it. We also treat negation, exceptions, and background axioms, where normal-form uniqueness still decides equivalence but counting is open.
item.dc:creator: Sherzod Turaev, Mary John

item.title: Regular Separability for Bidirected VASS
item.description: arXiv:2611.03313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The regular separability problem asks, given two languages, whether there exists a regular language that contains one of them and is disjoint from the other. We study regular separability for bidirected VASS. We first show that the problem remains Ackermann-complete when the input consists of two languages recognised by bidrected VASS. To find a subclass of VASS in which the problem has lower complexity we define alphabetically bidirected VASS as ones where bidirectedness is also visible in the input letters. Our main result establishes that regular separability for alphabetically bidirected VASS is EXPSPACE-complete. The key to this result is that, in this setting, regular separability coincides with disjointness. As a first ingredient in this equivalence, we also show that for alphabetically bidirected Z-VASS, regular separability and disjointness are equivalent. Consequently, regular separability for these systems is in polynomial-time. In fact, it is log-space inter-reducible with non-solvability of integer linear Diophantine equation systems. Finally, we observe that the picture changes dramatically in the presence of a zero test, namely, we show that regular separability for alphabetically bidirected one-counter automata is undecidable.
item.dc:creator: {\L}ukasz Orlikowski, Georg Zetzsche

item.title: Private Uniform Language Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.00797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study uniform language generation under approximate differential privacy. Given a uniformly bounded number of distinct examples from an unknown target language, a generator must produce infinitely many new examples from that language with probability one while protecting the privacy of its input. We introduce a new combinatorial dimension termed the nested branching dimension and prove that a language class is privately uniformly generatable if and only if both its closure dimension and nested branching dimension are finite. Previous work characterizes non-private uniform generation by the finiteness of the closure dimension alone. Our results therefore identify an additional combinatorial obstruction imposed by privacy.
item.dc:creator: Di Wang, Peng Ye

item.title: Maximal input entropy for binary two-deletion and two-insertion channels
item.description: arXiv:2611.01064v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Under uniform transmission, we determine the received binary words that maximize input entropy for two-deletion and two-insertion channels. For two deletions the maximizers are exactly the two alternating words at every positive received length. For two insertions the same conclusion holds from received length five onward; we give all smaller cases and exact maximal values. The proof combines an embedding-count identity organized by runs with strict convexity estimates, and a grouping of two-position deletion masks. For every insertion radius we give the complete positive embedding histogram of an alternating received word. We also determine its three-deletion histogram for every length, and certify all three-deletion maximizers through received length twelve and all three-insertion maximizers through length eighteen by exact integer comparison. These computations give precise three-error conjectures with their small-length exceptions.
item.dc:creator: Haobo Ma, Wenlin Zhang

item.title: A Circuit Complexity Trichotomy For Regular Languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.03615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish a trichotomy for the non-uniform, unbounded-fan-in circuit complexity of regular languages: the complexity of every regular language lies in exactly one of $O(1)$, $\Omega(\log n)\cap O(\log n\log\log n)$, or $\Omega(n)\cap O(n)$. Our main technical contribution is a characterization of the sublinear class in terms of algebra, word congruences, regular expressions, and logic. This class consists precisely of the regular languages computable by constant-depth circuits of size $O(\log^2 n)$, or, equivalently, by circuits of size $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and depth $O((\log\log n)^2)$. Consequently, every regular language of sublinear circuit complexity is definable in $\mathrm{FO}^2[\Sigma,<,\mathrm{mod}]$, which is contained in wire-linear $\mathbf{AC}^0$. For each of the three classes, deciding membership is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$-complete when the language is specified by a nondeterministic finite automaton. We also obtain a corresponding classification for regular languages with a neutral letter.
item.dc:creator: Stefan G\"oller, Amaldev Manuel

item.title: Certified Splitting: Decidability and Anchor Supply for Maximal-Munch Tokenization
item.description: arXiv:2610.08854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A certificate is a window of bytes with an origin inside it such that, wherever the window occurs in a completely tokenizable input, the token covering the window's final byte begins at that origin. Certification is decided from the token set alone, and a certificate's occurrences mark where work may soundly begin. This paper decides certification and applies it to cuts, edits and audits. It is decided two ways, online with a completeness cutoff for literal vocabularies and offline through an armed-run verifier for arbitrary regular token sets. Either route, under a declared window budget, yields the anchor inventory, with a counterexample on each refutation. Cutting a completely tokenizable input at certified anchors and scanning the chunks independently reproduces the sequential segmentation, with no speculation or fixup pass. A tokenizability-preserving byte substitution moves boundaries only strictly between the certified anchors witnessed in the unchanged bytes on either side of it. For tokens of length at most L, an edit at p moves no boundary at or below p - L + 1. Cutting at every occurrence of a delimiter is sound exactly when it occurs only at token starts, and cutting after every occurrence exactly when it occurs only at token ends. Two instruments follow. The anchor-free span of a finite certified inventory is decided bounded or not with its exact supremum, three for the UTF-8 shape; and a differential auditor decides whether two token sets place different boundaries on an input both tokenize, with a differing input. Every theorem carries an executable check. Every measurement is a named program's output or arithmetic on such outputs, and each program ships with the paper or is pinned by commit in the munch library. That library's threaded scanner splits the archived campaign corpus at certified anchors and reproduces the sequential boundary stream byte for byte.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: Finitely Verifiable Segmentation: Decidability for Every Tokenizer with a Finite-State Verifier
item.description: arXiv:2610.30168v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A segmentation policy assigns to each byte string at most one segmentation into tokens. Call it finitely verifiable when a finite automaton over marked strings, bytes paired with boundary bits, accepts exactly the policy's own segmentations. The automaton judges a proposed segmentation and need not compute one. From a supplied verifier the paper gives constructive decisions for four questions, whether a window certifies a token boundary, whether the boundary gap is bounded, whether a mask can keep generation from dead-ending, and whether two policies are equivalent. The last three specialize limitedness, co-accessibility and the equivalence of single-valued transducers. The first refines the synchronizing cut of code theory, and two more ask whether a certified cut, or the cuts of an inventory, let each piece scan alone. The class sits strictly between the online-scannable policies and those with regular domains, and online scannability is decidable in polynomial time through Choffrut's theorem. Markings are length-preserving, so the class is exactly the rational segmentation policies, a normal form rather than a restriction. The class is closed under four pipeline operations, composition over a labeled stage, restriction to a regular schema, splitting at character-class changes, and byte-fallback union of literal policies. Each composite inherits the six decisions, and certificates transfer between stages under four laws. Under rational, unifilar, almost surely stopping finite-state sources, each mass of the weighted section is an exact rational, and so is each rate where expected length is positive. Maximal-munch lexing, canonical byte-pair encoding and two-mode WordPiece instantiate the interface, and the munch library implements all six decisions. Every theorem carries an executable check, and every reported statistic is a program's own output.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: More on Higher Order Busy Beaver Functions
item.description: arXiv:2507.20321v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we extend the Busy Beaver function to a class of higher order Busy Beaver functions based on Turing oracle machine. We prove some results about the relation between decidability of number theoretical formula and higher order Busy Beaver functions, and the relations between computability of max-min partial recursive functions, limit partial recursive functions and higher order Busy Beaver functions. We also present some conjectures on higher order Busy Beaver functions.
item.dc:creator: Zining Cao

item.title: Formal Evidence Generation for Assurance Cases for Robotic Software Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.03550v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robotics and Autonomous Systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, so that demonstrating their safety is essential. Assurance Cases (ACs) provide structured arguments supported by evidence, but generating and maintaining this evidence is labour-intensive, error-prone, and difficult to keep consistent as systems evolve. We present a model-based approach to systematically generating AC evidence by embedding formal verification into the assurance workflow. The approach addresses three challenges: systematically deriving formal assertions from natural language requirements using templates, orchestrating multiple formal verification tools to handle diverse property types, and integrating formal evidence production into the workflow. Leveraging RoboChart, a domain-specific modelling language with formal semantics, we combine model checking and theorem proving in our approach. Structured requirements are automatically transformed into formal assertions using predefined templates, and verification results are automatically integrated as evidence. Case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Fang Yan, Simon Foster, Ana Cavalcanti, Ibrahim Habli, James Baxter
